catalog_quote: Suprasegmental features are not mentioned in the Dictionary and Grammar and they are inadequately recorded in the field notes. However, it is clear that words have suprasegmental phonemes as a part of their makeup and that in many instances this is the sole phonemic contrast between words. These phonemes have been called "tone" because pitch seemed to be their most stable feature, but loudness (stress) is very much involved, and perhaps length as well. One noticeable feature is the way in which the toneme of a monosyllabic word affects the pitch and stress of the following word. The words listed below were studied both in isolation and in a frame--followed by the particle /ti/. In section 1 above two tonemes were listed, tentatively labelled high /´/ and low /`/. new_statements.rule_in_words: Kapau word prosody is analysed as lexical tone (tentatively two tonemes, high and low, contrasting minimal pairs such as /tʌ/ 'fire' vs 'this'); loudness/stress is described as bound up with the tonemes rather than as an independent, positionally fixed word stress; no rule for stress placement is given and the author says the analysis has barely begun. Elsewhere (p.96) /ɨ/ is said to be 'frequently stressed'. Lloyd 1973:40 independently states for Kapau 'Phonemic stress occurs, but has not been completely analysed.'
new_statements.exceptions: Toneme of a monosyllable perturbs pitch and stress of the following word (tested in frame with particle /ti/); up-glides associated with slight vowel lengthening; three tone patterns on monosyllables, three on disyllables, many on trisyllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tonemes; data studied in isolation and in a frame before /ti/. The Rosetta excerpt lacks pp. 103-109 (secs. 4.4 end, 5 Glottal stop, 6 Syllabic nasals), which by their titles do not treat stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All three sources describe the language under the name Kapau (= Hamtai, hamt1247, ISO hmt); Healey's own data are from Slate Creek near Bulolo (1958) plus NTM materials from the Aseki/Morobe side; Lloyd 1973 calls the language relatively uniform dialectally. No sub-variety glottocode needed.

sources.note: p.110 sec.7 TONE: words carry suprasegmental phonemes, often the sole contrast between words; called 'tone' because pitch is the most stable feature, 'but loudness (stress) is very much involved, and perhaps length as well'; two tonemes (high, low) tentatively; toneme of a monosyllable affects pitch and stress of the following word; analysis 'barely begun'. p.96: /ɨ/ 'is frequently stressed'. No positional stress rule given.

sources.citation: Lloyd, Richard G. 1973. The Angan language family. In Karl Franklin (ed.), The linguistic situation in the Gulf District and adjacent areas, Papua New Guinea (Pacific Linguistics C-26), 31-110. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: sec. 2.31 Kapau phonology (pp. 39-40, following Healey 1958 ms): 'Phonemic stress occurs, but has not been completely analysed.' (p.40). Family summary p.87: 'Tone and stress are combined in a complex unit which usually occurs in connection with the grammatical stem... Angaataha is like a "tone language" and the others are more "intonation languages".' p.95: Angan languages 'have complex supra-segmental systems, usually a combination of pitch and stress'.
'14 consonants, 7 vowels, and two tones (rising and falling)', citing Healey 1981 p.95; nothing on stress.
